title: Running Shoes for Flat Feet and Plantar Fasciitis
excerpt: Shoes for flat feet and plantar fasciitis: why comfort comes first, what research and the 2023 treatment guideline say, and stability and cushioned picks.
body:
Running Shoes for Flat Feet and Plantar Fasciitis

Updated November 2026. Prices are US list prices (MSRP) at the time of this update; retailers often sell for less.

If you have flat feet or plantar fasciitis, start with comfort. Choose the shoe that feels best and reduces your pain on the run. Stability shoes are one option, not a rule. Shoes are also only part of treatment: stretching, strengthening and sensible training changes matter at least as much. If heel pain persists, see a doctor or physiotherapist.

What the research says about flat feet and shoes

A one-year study of novice runners in Denmark (Nielsen et al., 2014, British Journal of Sports Medicine) gave everyone the same neutral shoe. Runners with pronated (flatter) feet were no more likely to get injured than runners with neutral feet. The same paper notes earlier research found that assigning motion-control, stability or neutral shoes based on foot shape did not reduce injuries.

Those studies looked at healthy runners, not people who already have heel pain. If you do have plantar fasciitis, the best shoe is the one that feels comfortable and doesn't aggravate it. For some runners that's a stability shoe; for others, a well-cushioned neutral shoe.

Treating plantar fasciitis

The American Physical Therapy Association's 2023 clinical practice guideline for heel pain recommends:

  • Stretching: plantar fascia and calf stretches for short-term pain relief.
  • Strengthening: exercises for the toe flexors, the muscles that turn the ankle in and out, and the calf. These improve pain and function more than stretching alone.
  • Manual therapy: hands-on treatment of the plantar fascia by a physiotherapist, for short-term pain relief.

Some people also find insoles or orthoses helpful; a podiatrist or physiotherapist can advise. See a doctor or physiotherapist if your pain persists, or if it is getting worse despite rest and these measures.

Choosing a shoe

  • Comfort first: try several shoes, ideally later in the day, and run a few steps in each.
  • A secure heel: many runners with heel pain prefer a shoe with a firm heel counter that holds the heel in place.
  • Enough cushioning: a well-cushioned shoe can make hard surfaces more comfortable while your heel settles.
  • Drop: some runners with heel pain find a moderate heel-to-toe drop more comfortable than a very low one. The evidence on drop is limited, so go by feel.
  • Change gradually: avoid switching suddenly to minimalist or zero-drop shoes while your heel is painful.
  • Replace worn shoes: do so when the cushioning feels flat or the outsole is worn.

Shoes worth trying

Stability options

  • Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25: Brooks's stability trainer, made in wide and extra-wide widths. Its successor, the GTS 26, is on preorder.
  • ASICS Gel-Kayano 33 ($170): ASICS's stability shoe, with a 40 mm heel stack and an 8 mm drop.
  • Saucony Guide 19 ($140): gentle stability from a wide base and raised sidewalls rather than a medial post, with a 6 mm drop.
  • New Balance Fresh Foam X 860v15 ($149.99): New Balance's stability trainer, with Fresh Foam X cushioning.
  • Hoka Arahi 8 ($150): Hoka's stability trainer.

Cushioned neutral options

  • Hoka Bondi 9 ($175): maximum cushioning, with a heel stack of about 43 mm and a 5 mm drop. It comes in wide sizes.
  • Brooks Ghost 18 ($150): a cushioned daily trainer made in narrow to extra-wide widths.

Other things that help

  • Increase mileage gradually, and cut back temporarily if your heel pain flares.
  • Some runners find softer surfaces, such as trails or a track, more comfortable while their heel settles.
  • Keep doing the stretching and strengthening exercises after the pain eases.

For more on fitting shoes when your feet are wide, see our guide to running shoes for wide feet.
